result.summary:
Independently re-derived from docs/agents/design/REQ-022.md itself (not CODE-DESIGNER's step-01-code-designer.json result.summary), against the live requirement text (docs/agents/requirements.yaml lines 1148-1182), the live schema (apps/bot/src/db/schema.ts), and the live implementation of registerForEvent (apps/bot/src/domain/registration.ts lines 109-216).

1. ZERO IMPLEMENTATION CODE (exhaustive). `grep -n '```' docs/agents/design/REQ-022.md` finds exactly three fenced pairs: lines 97-114 (`WithdrawDecisionInput` interface + `WithdrawOutcome` union + `decideWithdrawOutcome(...)` signature, bare `;`-terminated, no body), lines 135-142 (`withdrawRegistration(...)` signature only, bare `;`), lines 367-379 (`Catalog.withdraw` interface, nine `string;` field declarations with trailing comments, no assigned values). Read all three blocks directly: none contains an `if`/`return`/comparison/arithmetic statement — the decision table for `decideWithdrawOutcome` (rows 1-5) is stated entirely in prose/markdown-table form ("first match wins", described, never coded), exactly the discipline `.claude/agents/code-designer.md` requires after the REQ-016/REQ-017 FAILs for this same trap. No `.tsx`, no SQL beyond one-line English-language descriptions of a `SELECT`/`UPDATE` shape (never a runnable query string), no handler body code anywhere in the document.

2. TOKEN REFERENCES. Bot/backend design, no rendered UI. `grep -n 'var(--\|--color\|--space\|--font'` over the file returns zero matches — nothing to check against docs/Design system for AI agents/tokens/tokens.css, consistent with REQ-018/020/021 precedent for this surface.

3. registerForEvent MODIFICATION vs. REQ-020's S7 capacity guarantee -- TRACED PRECISELY against the live code (apps/bot/src/domain/registration.ts):
   - Line 115 opens `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})`.
   - Lines 117-129: the `events` row is locked `FOR UPDATE` inside that transaction -- this lock is what serializes ALL concurrent `registerForEvent` calls for a given event, which is the actual mechanism S7's capacity guarantee depends on (two concurrent registrations for the last seat cannot both proceed past this point simultaneously).
   - Lines 137-142 (today): `existingRows` is read (plain SELECT, no FOR UPDATE) -- STILL INSIDE the same `tx.transaction` callback, i.e. inside the events-lock's transaction span, AFTER the lock is acquired, BEFORE `decideRegistrationOutcome` is called (line 155).
   - The design's change (Sec3, points 1-2) is scoped EXACTLY to this existing read: it adds `id` to the selected columns and computes a normalized `existingAdmission` (withdrawn -> null, everything else passed through unchanged) from the SAME read, at the SAME point in the function, still inside the SAME `tx.transaction` callback, still after the events lock, still before the call to `decideRegistrationOutcome`. The design does not propose relocating this read, does not propose a second connection/transaction for it, and does not touch lines 117-129 (the lock acquisition) or lines 144-152 (admittedCount/seatsLeft computation, also unchanged, also computed under the same lock). VERDICT: the normalization stays fully inside the FOR UPDATE-locked transaction span -- it does not reopen REQ-020's closed race. `decideRegistrationOutcome` itself (lines 48-74) is confirmed byte-for-byte unreferenced by this design's diff -- only its caller's computed input changes, exactly as Sec3.3 states, verified against the actual function body, not asserted.
   - Non-blocking note for the record (not a design defect, not a capacity/S7 regression): registerForEvent's `existingRows` read at line 137-142 is a plain SELECT, not FOR UPDATE, both today and in this design (the design does not add a lock there, matching what already ships). This creates a theoretical READ COMMITTED TOCTOU window against a concurrent `withdrawRegistration` call racing the SAME registrations row (which does take its own FOR UPDATE lock, Sec2.2 step 1, in a separate transaction that never touches the events row). Traced the actual interleavings: in every case where `registerForEvent`'s decision would result in a write (the row-reuse UPDATE), that write targets the row by `id` and blocks on Postgres's ordinary lock semantics if a concurrent `withdrawRegistration` transaction on the same row is still in flight, then re-reads on wake; the two possible commit orderings both resolve to a safe last-committer-wins state (a second registration attempt on an already-admitted row degrades to "already-registered", a second withdrawal attempt on an already-withdrawn row degrades to "not-eligible") -- neither ordering can double-admit past capacity, because capacity is governed exclusively by the events-row lock and the live `admittedCount` COUNT under it (unchanged), and withdrawal only ever removes a row from that count, never adds one. This same unlocked-read pattern already exists in the shipped REQ-020 code (today's `existingRows` read is equally unlocked) -- the design does not introduce a new class of risk, it extends an existing pattern to a second writer. Filing as a MINOR issue for the record per Unblock-Everything's 'notice, don't fix here' boundary, not a FAIL: it is not a capacity/S7 regression and not something this design silently overlooked (the design's own Sec2.3 already reasons carefully about a related but distinct race -- checked-in-during-confirmation-window).

4. UPDATE-not-INSERT BRANCH -- verified against the live schema (apps/bot/src/db/schema.ts lines 242-300). `registrations.id` (line 245, uuid PK) and `createdAt` (lines 275-277, `timestamp("created_at",...).notNull().defaultNow()`) are real, named columns. The design's Sec3 point 3 UPDATE statement names exactly three columns in its SET clause -- `admission`, `source`, `qr_token` -- and Sec3.1 correctly states the Postgres semantics that an UPDATE leaves every unnamed column (including `id`, which is a PK and immutable by construction, and `created_at`) untouched. No `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` upsert pattern is introduced (confirmed absent from the design) which would risk a default-re-evaluation footgun. This is provably correct, not merely asserted.

5. CHECKED-IN REFUSAL -- verified against the live schema. `checkedInAt` (schema.ts line 256, nullable `timestamptz`) and the CHECK constraint `chk_registrations_checked_in_only_if_admitted` (lines 295-298: `checked_in_at IS NULL OR admission = 'admitted'`) match the design's Sec2.1 row 3 exactly: a non-null `checkedInAt` refuses withdrawal (`"checked-in"` outcome), checked before the eligibility row, correctly reasoned as never masking a distinct case because the CHECK constraint guarantees a checked-in row is always `admission='admitted'` (schema-enforced, not just assumed by the design).

6. CONFIRMATION UX -- Sec4.1-4.3 traced: the `/withdraw` command (Sec4.1) shows the confirm/cancel `InlineKeyboard` (Sec4.1 step 7) ONLY when `decideWithdrawOutcome` already found the registration eligible (step 6 short-circuits refusals before any prompt is shown); the accidental-single-tap risk is closed because a single Telegram tap on `/withdraw <event_id>` alone can only ever produce a PROMPT, never a write -- the write requires a second, distinct tap on the `withdraw:confirm:<id>` callback (Sec4.2), which re-derives ownership/checked-in/eligibility fresh (Sec2.3) rather than trusting the prompt's earlier read. The dismiss path (Sec4.3, `withdraw:cancel:<id>`) is explicitly stated to make ZERO domain calls of any kind -- no read, no write, no audit call -- making "dismissing leaves the row completely unchanged" true by construction rather than by a refusal branch that could have a bug in it. Confirmed no partial-state path exists: the only write in the entire design (Sec2.2 step 4's single UPDATE) is reached exclusively through the confirm callback -> `withdrawRegistration` -> outcome.kind==="withdrawn" branch.

7. AUDIT-LOG INTEGRATION (AC5) -- Sec2.2 step 5: exactly one `writeAuditLog` call, reached only on the single `"withdrawn"`-producing branch (step 3 returns early for every other outcome, zero write/zero audit call), inside the same `db.transaction` as the step-4 UPDATE. Matches S8 ("exactly one AuditLog row, same transaction, atomic") and matches the existing `writeAuditLog`/`registerForEvent` discipline this codebase already follows (verified against the live `registerForEvent`'s own single `writeAuditLog` call at lines 201-208, same pattern).

8. `/my`-DOESN'T-EXIST-YET SCOPING JUDGMENT (Sec0). Read Sec0 in full and weighed it independently, same standard I applied to REQ-021's own doesn't-exist-yet judgment. I agree with option "build a standalone /withdraw <event_id> command now" as correct, not merely defensible, for reasons beyond citing precedent: (a) every one of this requirement's 5 ACs tests domain-level state transitions (admission flips, refusal rules, row-reuse, audit rows) that are fully exercised by a typed-argument command exactly as they would be by a future /my list-row button -- the entry point's shape (`ctx.match` argument vs. a callback_data payload carrying the same id) is cosmetic relative to what the ACs actually verify, confirmed by reading Sec4.4's own reasoning for why the callback payload is a `registrationId` (which is exactly the value a future /my row would also need to carry); (b) unlike a genuinely premature build, this does not require inventing any REQ-024 concept to make work -- `/withdraw <event_id>` needs only `resolveActingUser` and a plain `(event_id, user_id)` lookup, both of which exist today, so nothing about /my is being second-guessed or pre-built; (c) the alternative -- deferring all of REQ-022's domain logic until REQ-024 ships -- would either stall REQ-023 (auto-promotion has no trigger without a real withdrawal path, stated in the requirement's own sequencing rationale) or force REQ-024 to absorb REQ-022's full scope, which the dependency graph in requirements.yaml does not authorize this document to redraw. I find no reason for ORCH/REQ-ANALYST to reconsider the sequencing; Sec0 point 4's forward note to REQ-024 is correctly left as a non-binding recommendation rather than an assertion this document has no authority to make.

9. AC-TO-DESIGN-ELEMENT MAP -- re-derived against the live requirement text (docs/agents/requirements.yaml lines 1176-1181), not trusted from Sec7's own table: AC1 (confirmation required, dismiss leaves row unchanged) -> Sec4 (item 6 above). AC2 (withdrawing admitted -> admission='withdrawn', seats-left +1 at next read) -> Sec2.2 step 4 + Sec1's restated, unchanged `computeSeatsLeft` proof (counts only 'admitted' rows; verified this claim against REQ-017's own shipped `computeSeatsLeft`, not re-read here since Sec1 states it is byte-for-byte unchanged and no diff to that function appears anywhere in this design). AC3 (checked_in_at non-null refused, row unchanged) -> Sec2.1 row 3 + Sec2.2 step 3 (item 5 above). AC4 (re-registration UPDATEs the same row, same PK, same created_at) -> Sec3 + Sec3.1 (item 4 above). AC5 (exactly one audit_log row) -> Sec2.2 step 5 (item 7 above). All 5 map to concrete, non-deferred design elements; no "TBD"/deferral language found anywhere in the document (checked Sec6's four open questions individually -- each states the ambiguity AND the design's chosen resolution or explicit deferral-to-a-named-future-owner, never a silent gap in an AC-relevant area).

Verdict: PASS. No check failed.

issues.description: docs/agents/design/REQ-022.md's registerForEvent modification (Sec3) keeps the existing, already-shipped pattern of reading existingAdmission/existingRegistrationId via a plain (non-FOR-UPDATE) SELECT inside the events-locked transaction. This does not regress S7 (capacity is governed solely by the events-row lock plus the live admittedCount COUNT under it, both untouched) and is not a new risk class (the same unlocked-read pattern already ships in REQ-020's current registerForEvent). But REQ-022 does introduce a second writer (withdrawRegistration, via its own FOR UPDATE on the registrations row) racing that same unlocked read for the first time. Every traced interleaving resolves safely (last-committer-wins degrades to an existing refusal outcome, never a double-write or over-capacity admit), so this is not blocking -- filed for the record so REQ-023 (auto-promotion, the next writer to touch this same row) inherits awareness of the pattern rather than rediscovering it.

Carried forward from CODE-DESIGNER's own step-01 handoff (not a new finding): docs/agents/design/REQ-022.md Sec6 open question 1 (new handlers/withdraw.ts vs. extending handlers/registration.ts) is correctly left to BACKEND-DEV's judgment since both options satisfy every acceptance criterion identically -- named explicitly, not silently resolved. No action needed at this gate.
